name: Yusuf Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a producer, mostly electronic and indie pop. I've got a small studio in a shared warehouse unit on Canal Road, and I produce records for artists who can't afford the big studios. Tuesday and Thursday evenings I teach music technology at the city college. About twice a month I play live sets with a modular synth rig, which is a wall of knobs and cables.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of your day is on a screen, would you say?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of it, honestly. Eighty per cent is me at a laptop, arranging, mixing, sending files back and forth with artists. I use AI tools every day already: to split a rough phone recording into separate parts, to get a first draft of a mix, to clean up vocals. The tools didn't replace me; they replaced the boring three hours before the interesting part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say already: the tools are good assistants and bad artists. I'd probably make a video for my students showing what they can and can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's basically today with slightly better software. My clients still need someone with taste to tell them the chorus is too long. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep producing about six records a year and keep the college classes. I'd put some of my savings into a better pair of studio speakers I've wanted for ages. And I'd keep trying every new tool that comes out, because that's half the fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit disappointed, if I'm honest, because I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed? Most people would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get that. But I've built my whole way of working around these tools, and I was looking forward to them getting better. A plateau means I keep my job and my clients, and also that the clever mixing assistant I wanted never shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone around you who'd still have a hard time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Ama does voice-overs for adverts. Even a plateau takes some of the cheap radio spots away from her. She's already noticed it this year.

say: I'd say the tools are **good assistants** and bad artists.
I'd make a **video for students** showing what the tools can and can't do.
think: For me it's basically **today** with slightly better software.
Clients still need someone with **taste** to tell them the chorus is too long.
do: Keep producing about **six records** a year and teaching two college evenings.
Spend some savings on new **studio speakers** he's wanted for ages.
feel: **Calm**, and a little disappointed that the tools stop improving.
S0.quote: A plateau means I keep my job and my clients, and also that the clever mixing assistant I wanted never shows up.
fieldNote: Yusuf already uses AI **every day**, so a plateau changes almost nothing for him.
He's the rare person who'd be **disappointed** by AI stalling.
He notices friends like Ama in **voice-over work** still losing small jobs.

steps.text: Keep producing six records a year from the Canal Road unit
Buy the new pair of studio monitor speakers from savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly: the tools are great, the ownership is the problem. If a handful of companies own the machines and the music they learned from, musicians get squeezed. I'd push for artist-owned platforms and a proper licensing system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the bottom of my market falls out. The bedroom artists who pay me for mixing will get a decent AI mix for a tenner. The ones who stay will want something only a person in a room can give them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rebuild my offer around that. I'd stop selling plain mixing and sell full production days with the artist in the room, maybe at a higher rate. I'd turn my college course into a class on producing with AI, which colleges will want. And I'd book more live sets, because a modular rig on a stage is the one thing nobody can download.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited too, which I know is a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What share of your income is plain mixing today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third, maybe less. That's the part I'd expect to lose within two years. I'd lose the third of my income that was mixing, and that's the third I enjoyed least anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said artist-owned platforms. What would you actually do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a small co-op of producers in the warehouse already talking about a shared label. I'd put some savings into it and help set up the licensing side. Maybe it fails, but I'd rather try than complain.

say: I'd say the tools are fine and **ownership** is the real problem.
I'd push publicly for **artist-owned platforms** and a fair licensing system.
think: I think the **bottom of my market**, plain mixing, falls out within two years.
Clients who stay will want what only a **person in the room** can give.
do: Replace plain mixing with **full production days** at a higher rate.
Turn the college course into a class on **producing with AI**.
Put some savings into a **producers' co-op** label in the warehouse.
feel: **Uneasy** and excited at the same time.
S1.quote: I'd lose the third of my income that was mixing, and that's the third I enjoyed least anyway.
fieldNote: Yusuf would lose about **a third** of his income, yet sees a way to rebuild around it.
His progressive outlook shows in his push for **shared ownership**, not in refusing the tools.
He moves **first**: changing his offer before clients leave.

steps.text: Rewrite the college course as a class on producing with AI
Put savings into the warehouse producers' co-op label
Help set up shared licensing rules for the co-op
Book twice as many paid live modular sets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, fast, because a lot of creative people are about to have nothing. I'd say the AI companies should pay into it. And I'd say it in the same breath as admitting I use their tools every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think production as a job is mostly over by 2029. If a machine can make a finished, great-sounding record from a voice note, artists won't need me. What's left is live performance and teaching people face to face, and those have about three years before robots matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch to live work almost straight away: more modular sets, plus building live shows for other artists, because that's hands-on and messy. I'd ask the college for more teaching hours. And I'd stop spending on studio gear and keep my savings as cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head says I'll adapt, my stomach isn't so sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said live work has three years before robots matter. What happens after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't think people go to a club to watch a robot turn knobs. The robot could do it, sure. People pay to watch a person take a risk on stage, and a robot taking a risk isn't interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you sell or give up first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse unit, probably. It's cheap, but if I'm not producing, I don't need it. I'd move the modular rig into my flat and rehearse there.

say: I'd call for a **basic income**, paid into by AI companies.
I'd say it while **admitting** I use their tools every day.
think: I think **production** as a job is mostly over by 2029.
What's left is **live performance** and face-to-face teaching, with about three years before robots matter.
do: Switch to **live work** straight away, including building live shows for other artists.
Ask the college for **more teaching hours**.
Stop buying gear and keep **savings as cash**.
feel: **Anxious**: his head says he'll adapt, his stomach isn't sure.
S2.quote: People pay to watch a person take a risk on stage, and a robot taking a risk isn't interesting.
fieldNote: Fast AGI ends the **core of his job**, but he has a clear move to live work.
He's betting on people valuing **human risk** on stage, even after robots arrive.
His **savings** and early moves give him a sense of control.

steps.text: Switch from studio production to building live shows for artists
Give up the Canal Road warehouse unit and rehearse at home
Freeze gear spending and hold savings in cash
Campaign for a basic income funded by AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for musicians to organise. I'd talk about the co-op idea everywhere, in my classes, online, at gigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is enough to move gradually. Production fades around 2030, and I'd already have the live side built by then. Robots for hands-on work around 2034 feel far away from a club stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep producing for the next three years while it pays, using the newest tools so I'm fast. Then I'd move my money from studio gear into a mobile live rig and a van. I'd also help set up the co-op label so there's something musicians own when the shift comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. I can see a path through this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a second-hand one. If live work is where the money moves, I need to get my rig to other cities without paying a driver. A second-hand van is the most important music investment I'd make in the next five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as the college wants me. Teaching keeps me honest about what I actually know.

say: I'd say **five years** is time for musicians to organise.
I'd talk up the **co-op label** in classes, online and at gigs.
think: **Production** fades around 2030, and I'd have the live side built by then.
**Robots** around 2034 feel far from a club stage.
do: Keep producing for **three more years** using the newest tools for speed.
Move money from studio gear into a **mobile live rig** and a used van.
feel: **Uneasy**, because he can see a path through it.
S3.quote: A second-hand van is the most important music investment I'd make in the next five years.
fieldNote: Five years lets Yusuf **sequence** the move: production now, live work later.
His most concrete purchase is a **second-hand van**, which says a lot about his plan.
He still expects to **lose production** income, but feels well ahead of it.

steps.text: Use the newest AI tools to speed up production for three years
Buy a second-hand van and a mobile live rig
Help launch the warehouse co-op label before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get the rules right, and I'd say the rules matter more than the tech. Who owns the music, who gets paid when a machine copies a style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm thirty-seven. I'd have had a full decade of producing with better and better tools, then moved into live work and teaching. That doesn't scare me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and grow it. I'd take on a second studio room and hire an assistant for a few years, because the work would grow before it shrinks. I'd keep putting money in the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Kind of looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hire an assistant, when assistants are what AI replaces first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd hire a young producer for three or four years, train them, and be honest that it's a bridge. I'd rather give a young producer three good years of training than pretend nothing is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your calm here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the co-op fails and everything ends up on two big platforms. Then even live work gets squeezed by whoever sells the tickets.

say: I'd say the **rules** on ownership and payment matter more than the tech.
I'd point out **ten years** is plenty of time to get those rules right.
think: By **thirty-seven** I'd have moved from producing into live work and teaching.
That **gradual shift** doesn't scare me much.
do: Take on a **second studio room** and hire an assistant for a few years.
Keep **investing** in the warehouse co-op label.
S4.quote: I'd rather give a young producer three good years of training than pretend nothing is coming.
fieldNote: With a decade, Yusuf sees **growth** before decline and wants to ride it.
He's honest that a new hire would be a **bridge job**.
His one fear is **platform control**, not the technology.

steps.text: Rent a second studio room and hire a junior producer
Keep producing and teaching college evenings as now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything shared before it hits. What would help is a basic income floor, and real money for artist-owned co-ops so musicians own a piece of the new tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about students. My college students are nineteen and paying for a course in a job that might change completely. I'd want colleges to be honest with them, and to teach live skills alongside the software.

headlineQuote: The tools didn't replace me; they replaced the boring three hours before the interesting part.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** electronic producer who also teaches music technology and plays live modular sets.
He uses **AI tools daily** and treats them as assistants, not threats.
As a **progressive**, he worries about who owns the tools, and backs a producers' co-op.
He plans to move from **production** into live work and teaching as AI improves.
Only **fast AGI** makes him anxious, because there'd be no time to build shared alternatives.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build anything shared first.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** floor, and funding for **artist-owned co-ops**.
